resources.string: Connect a device in Fastboot mode to use these tools.
Connect a device in Recovery or ADB Sideload mode to use these tools.

Protocol mode is unknown until a handshake. Descriptors distinguish an ADB class interface from a Fastboot class one, but not Android from Recovery or Sideload, nor bootloader Fastboot from fastbootd.
Devices have not been examined yet.
The system reports no USB devices at all. Check OTG, the cable and the adapter: without a device there is nothing to ask permission for.
The system reports %1$d USB device(s), but none of them exposes an ADB or Fastboot interface.
This host reports no USB host mode support, so no device can be examined.
Ask the device who it is
Command, as the device knows it
Sent %2$d s ago, still no answer: %1$s

The exchange frame is lost. The device is still waiting for the bytes of the previous command, so the next one would go nowhere — that is why the lane refuses. Only a fresh claim of the interface clears it. The device itself is not touched and loses nothing.
The list is incomplete. Variables read before the exchange broke off: %1$d
%1$s was named more than once with different values: %2$s
Lines that could not be parsed: %1$d — kept in the diagnostics

There is no command list here on purpose: what Fastboot offers is known to the device, and a refusal is its answer, not our error. Two things the wire itself cannot carry are named rather than sent silently altered: a command outside ASCII, and one longer than 4096 bytes. The lane is shown because Fastboot has exactly one and losing its framing is sticky — a second command would then go nowhere.
The device buffer was not touched: not a single byte was sent.
The download buffer now holds something; flashing from it is not safe unless the device confirmed the whole payload.

A button here does not reach the lane on its own: it builds the same string and hands it to the same entry point as the free-form command field, so the engine is one and they have nowhere to diverge. The destructive commands — flash:, erase: and format: — live on the Write tab next to the lock state, because the lock is what decides the form of the warning. The confirmation there is not permission: the command reaches the device unchanged either way. A slot switch can be acknowledged by the device without being made, so the slot is read back separately.
A refusal is the device saying it did not carry the command out. It is not proof that the partition is intact: what is known is what the device said, not what it managed to do before refusing.
%1$s → the device answered OKAY, but %2$s was requested and the device reports %3$s. That does not count as a switch.
%1$s → the device left without answering (%2$d ms). For a reboot that is expected, not a lost link.
What the partition now holds is unknown. It may have been left half-written, and its contents cannot be relied on.
%1$s → the exchange never started: %2$s. The device never saw this command.
A refusal is the device saying the lock is untouched. It is not proof: what is known is what the device said, not what it managed to do before refusing.
The lock state is unknown, and so is the state of user data with it: changing the lock normally wipes the device. This is the worst unknown state Fastboot has.
This will be sent: %1$s. If the device carries it out, the previous contents of the partition are gone and there is nothing here to restore them from.

The lock is confirmed, so the expected outcome is this: the device will almost certainly refuse with FAIL and the partition will not change. On some bootloaders the whole payload is transferred first and the refusal only comes after. The command is sent unchanged regardless — the decision belongs to the device, not to the app.

The confirmation here is not permission: the command reaches the device unchanged either way, only the deliberateness of the tap differs. The confirmation word is asked for only when the lock is confirmed; "unknown" does not count as locked, otherwise not knowing would turn into forbidding. The free-form command field is untouched by all of this and runs the same commands without a prompt. Flashing the buffer sends whatever the download buffer holds right now — if this app put it there, that is a pattern for checking byte accounting, not an image.
fetch: usually lives in fastbootd, not in the bootloader. Sending it from here is allowed — the device answers.
%1$s was NOT read in full. Bytes: %2$d. This cannot be passed off as the partition — a missing piece is indistinguishable from zeros inside it.
Partitions named: %1$d, confirmed by a substantive field: %2$d. Size, type or the logical flag confirm one; has-slot alone does not — devices answer it for names they do not have.
The plan ran in full. Steps: %1$d / %2$d
The plan stopped. Completed steps: %1$d / %2$d. The device is left between "before" and "after" — part of it happened, the rest did not.
The package has started reaching the device: there is nothing left to cancel.
Recovery ended the transfer (DONEDONE). This says the host handed everything over, and nothing about the install.
Recovery closed the stream at %1$d%% of confirmed coverage. Nearly complete is not complete.
The stream broke after the package started reaching the device, at %1$d%% of confirmed coverage. The state of the device is unknown whatever that number looks like.
Cancelled before a single byte of the package reached the device.
The device is not answering from Sideload: %1$s
Read the Recovery verdict: only Recovery can say whether it installed.
Choose a ZIP to transfer. When the transfer ends, check the installation result on the device in Recovery.
Connect a device in Recovery and open Apply update from ADB, then choose a ZIP here.
Copying %2$s into the app so blocks can be read in any order. Bytes copied: %1$d. The device has not been touched.
Recovery asks for blocks in its own order and may ask for the same one twice, so a file that can only be read front to back is copied first. Nothing reaches the device during the copy.
Shows the transfer that is running so the system does not stop it while the app is in the background.
